sections.title: What RA is and how it presents

blocks.text: Rheumatoid arthritis is a **chronic, relapsing–remitting inflammatory arthritis** of synovium (joints, tendon sheaths and bursae). Prevalence is roughly **0.8–1%** in Europe and the Indian subcontinent, the highest rate is in **Pima Indians (5%)**, and women outnumber men about **3 : 1**. It usually presents between 30 and 50 years of age, though it can start at any age.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis as one chain
items: A trigger (**smoking**, infection) modifies self-proteins by **citrullination** in a host carrying susceptible **HLA-DRβ1** alleles (HLA-DR4).
T cells help B cells make autoantibodies: **rheumatoid factor (RF)** and **anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPA)**.
Macrophages release **TNF, IL-1 and IL-6**, which drive synovial fibroblast proliferation and new vessel growth.
The inflamed synovium spreads over cartilage as **pannus**; **RANKL** and **M-CSF** activate osteoclasts, producing **marginal erosions**.
Smoking also predicts more severe disease and a weaker response to treatment.

blocks.title: The typical joint picture
rows: Symmetrical, small joints of hands, wrists and feet; large joints can join later
MCPs, PIPs, wrists, MTPs, ankles, cervical spine; **DIPs spared**; thoracolumbar spine spared
Usually insidious over weeks to months (~70% of cases)
Prolonged early-morning stiffness (often over 30 min), worse after rest, eased by activity
Warm, tender, **boggy** synovial swelling; PIP swelling gives spindle-shaped fingers
Fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, flu-like aches

blocks.title: Less typical ways RA can begin
items: **Acute, explosive onset** with severe morning stiffness and pitting oedema of the limbs, more often in older people.
**Polymyalgia-like** proximal girdle stiffness.
**Palindromic** pattern (~5%): attacks of a red, swollen joint lasting 24–48 h that settle completely; about half later develop RA, more likely if RF or ACPA is positive.
About 10% start with a single large joint (knee, shoulder) or with **carpal tunnel syndrome**.
A systemic illness with few joint symptoms at first.

blocks.title: Deformities of long-standing, poorly controlled RA
rows: Fingers drift ulnarwards at the MCP joints, often with small-muscle wasting
The **PIP joint over-extends** while the DIP bends (MCP usually also bent)
The **PIP joint stays bent** and the DIP is pushed back into extension
The ulnar head subluxes dorsally at the distal radio-ulnar joint and wears through the 4th and 5th extensor tendons
MTP subluxation gives **cock-up toes**, painful exposed MTP heads, bursae and callosities
Valgus heel and flat foot from **tibialis posterior** rupture
**Baker's (popliteal) cyst**; rupture gives calf pain and swelling that mimics DVT

blocks.note: Look at: ulnar deviation with small-muscle wasting and swelling of wrists, extensor sheaths, MCPs and PIPs (A); swan-neck fingers (B).
Diagram of the rheumatoid hand: ulnar deviation, boutonnière and swan-neck fingers, Z-thumb, MCP and PIP swelling.

blocks.text: **Inflammatory vs mechanical pain:** inflammatory joints are worst after rest and loosen with use; osteoarthritic (mechanical) joints are worst with use and ease with rest.

Redness of the skin over a rheumatoid joint is unusual. A single joint that is red, or flaring out of proportion to the rest, is **septic arthritis until proven otherwise**: aspirate before calling it a flare.

sections.title: Differential diagnosis of an inflammatory polyarthritis

blocks.text: **Polyarthritis** means pain and swelling in **five or more joints or joint groups**. Inflammatory disease is suggested by early-morning stiffness, worsening with inactivity, and soft synovial swelling with tenderness. RA rarely presents as a monoarthritis.

blocks.title: Telling the polyarthritides apart
rows: Symmetrical MCPs + PIPs, wrists, MTPs; DIPs spared
Prolonged morning stiffness, nodules, RF/ACPA positive
Dactylitis, enthesitis, nail pitting or onycholysis (skin psoriasis may be absent); arthritis mutilans can mimic severe RA
Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes; osteophytes on X-ray; short stiffness
Large joints of the **lower limb**, asymmetrical
Rubella, hepatitis B, parvovirus (erythrovirus); rarely lasts beyond about 6 weeks; ACPA negative
Young woman; arthralgia with joints that often look normal

blocks.text: Quick screen: RA becomes **unlikely** if the pattern is asymmetrical, the **DIPs** are involved, or there is **no morning stiffness**.
Painful, enlarged **DIP** joints point away from RA, towards osteoarthritis (Heberden's nodes) or psoriatic arthritis.
**Osteophytes** belong to osteoarthritis and are absent in RA; RA changes are more widespread because the whole synovial lining is inflamed.

The **2010 ACR/EULAR criteria** are applied to a patient with at least one clinically swollen joint not better explained by another disease. Four domains are scored and a total of **6 or more out of 10** classifies the patient as **definite RA**. Because they do not need erosions or extra-articular disease, they work in **early arthritis**; a patient with typical erosions and long-standing disease can still be classed as RA.
Only the **highest** category in each domain counts. Joints and serology carry most weight (up to 5 and 3 points); duration and acute-phase reactants add 1 point each.
A **seronegative** patient can still reach 6: more than 10 joints including a small one (5) plus symptoms beyond 6 weeks (1) is enough. Negative RF/ACPA does not exclude RA.

These are **classification** criteria built for research. In practice the diagnosis of RA is **clinical**: no single test proves it, and you combine the joint pattern, stiffness, nodules, blood tests and imaging.

Extra-articular disease affects about **18–41%** of patients. It is commonest in **long-standing, seropositive, erosive** RA, but can appear at onset (especially in men). Most features arise from **serositis**, **granulomas/nodules** or **vasculitis**.

blocks.title: Extra-articular RA by system
rows: Over pressure points and extensor surfaces (elbow, fingers, Achilles); almost only in RF/ACPA-positive patients; can ulcerate or become infected; also in pleura, lung, pericardium, sclera
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (secondary Sjögren's, commonest); episcleritis; **scleritis** and peripheral ulcerative keratitis (painful red eye, sight-threatening); scleromalacia
Pleural effusion, interstitial fibrosis (restrictive), nodules that may cavitate, bronchiolitis/bronchiectasis, **Caplan's syndrome** (nodules with pneumoconiosis)
Pericarditis/effusion; nodules causing heart block or bundle branch block; rarely myocarditis, aortitis
Entrapment (median nerve commonest; ulnar, lateral popliteal, tarsal tunnel); symmetrical sensory neuropathy; **mononeuritis multiplex** with vasculitis
Normocytic normochromic anaemia, thrombocytosis, eosinophilia; Felty's syndrome
Nail-fold infarcts, digital arteritis, leg ulcers, pyoderma gangrenosum, rarely visceral arteritis

blocks.title: Felty's syndrome
items: Triad: **RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia** (often thrombocytopenia and anaemia too).
Typical patient: long-standing, **seropositive** (high-titre RF), deforming but **inactive** joint disease.
Also leg ulcers, recurrent infections, lymphadenopathy, skin pigmentation, abnormal LFTs.
HLA-DR4 is found in about 95% of patients with Felty's, versus 50–75% of RA overall.

blocks.text: A rheumatoid pleural effusion has a **very low glucose** and low complement.
**Mononeuritis multiplex** in RA means nerve-trunk infarction from **systemic vasculitis**, a poor prognostic sign.

blocks.note: Look at: rheumatoid nodules at the elbow with olecranon bursitis; nodules felt inside and outside the bursa.

blocks.text: Dry, gritty eyes are the commonest eye problem, but a **painful** red eye in RA suggests scleritis or peripheral ulcerative keratitis, which can threaten sight.

Diagnosis is mainly **clinical**; tests support it, measure activity and track damage and drug safety. ESR and CRP are usually raised and follow disease activity, but they are **normal in about a third** of patients, especially when few joints are involved.

blocks.title: Autoantibodies in RA
rows: Antibody (usually IgM) against the Fc portion of IgG
High titre means more severe and extra-articular disease; titre barely changes with activity, so not used to monitor
Antibodies to peptides in which arginine has been converted to citrulline by peptidylarginine deiminase
Preferred over RF; can appear years before symptoms; predicts more severe progression

blocks.title: Positive RF outside RA, grouped by how often it is found
rows: SLE (~30%); healthy people aged over 65 (~20%); tuberculosis (~15%)

blocks.title: Other tests
items: FBC: normocytic normochromic anaemia and thrombocytosis with active disease.
Synovial fluid: turbid from white cells (neutrophil-rich) but **sterile** in uncomplicated RA.
X-rays of hands and feet: often normal early; then soft-tissue swelling, **periarticular osteopenia**, joint-space narrowing, **marginal erosions** and cysts. Used to measure damage.
**Ultrasound or MRI** when synovitis is uncertain on examination; ultrasound also confirms a Baker's cyst.
Suspected atlanto-axial disease: lateral cervical X-rays in **flexion and extension** plus MRI.

blocks.text: **DAS28** combines swollen and tender joint counts across 28 joints (upper limbs and knees), the ESR (or CRP) and the patient's global assessment on a 0–100 visual analogue scale. Interpretation: **above 5.1 high activity, 2.6–5.1 moderate, below 2.6 remission**. The HAQ questionnaire scores function.

blocks.title: Monitoring drug safety
items: Baseline and follow-up: urinalysis, FBC, urea and creatinine, LFTs, chest X-ray.
DMARD blood tests usually every 2 weeks for the first 6 weeks, then monthly for 3 months, then every 3 months.
Hydroxychloroquine instead needs checks of **visual function**.

blocks.note: Look at: hand X-ray in early RA with erosions at the thumb, middle MCP joints and ulnar styloid.
Compare: OA hand (osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, narrowing) with RA hand (periarticular erosions and osteopenia).

blocks.text: Antibody figures differ between books: Davidson gives ACPA sensitivity ~70% with specificity over 95% and RF ~70%; KC Essentials quotes ACPA ~80% sensitive and ~90% specific, and Kumar gives RF 75–80%. Follow **Davidson** in the exam.
NICE: refer anyone with **persistent synovitis** even if RF, ACPA and inflammatory markers are all negative.

blocks.title: Atlanto-axial (C1–C2) subluxation
items: Synovitis erodes the **transverse ligament** behind the odontoid peg, so C1 slips on C2.
Cervical instability is found in 30–40% of RA patients; cord compression is rare but can follow minor trauma or neck manipulation, and can be fatal.
Suspect it with **new occipital headache** and **electric-shock or tingling sensations in the arms**; onset is often insidious.
Power and reflexes are hard to judge in deformed limbs, so sensory and upper motor neurone signs matter most.
Image with flexion/extension lateral X-rays and MRI; cord compression needs **urgent neurosurgical** stabilisation.

blocks.note: Look at: lateral cervical spine films; the gap between odontoid peg and anterior arch of atlas widens in flexion and closes in extension.

blocks.title: Other complications
rows: Rheumatoid joints infect more easily; on immunosuppression fever and local signs may be muted
Rare, long-standing disease; presents with **nephrotic syndrome**; RA is the commonest cause of secondary AA amyloid
Normocytic with thrombocytosis in active disease; **microcytic** if iron deficient from NSAID GI blood loss
More common in long-standing RA; suspect if lymphadenopathy **persists**
Accelerated atherosclerosis (cytokines on endothelium, plus NSAIDs, steroids and classic risk factors) raises MI risk and mortality
Tendon rupture from tenosynovitis, subluxation and fixed deformity
Higher overall infection risk, increased further by DMARDs and biologics

blocks.title: Markers of a worse prognosis
rows: Many joints and extra-articular organs involved, subcutaneous nodules
RF and ACPA positive, especially high-titre RF

blocks.text: Before **general anaesthesia** (intubation) or upper GI endoscopy, image the cervical spine in RA to find instability and avoid cord injury.

Aims: **suppress inflammation, control symptoms and prevent joint damage**, aiming for remission (**treat to target**, measured by DAS28 and CRP). Damage starts early, so DMARDs are begun as soon as possible, ideally within 3 months of onset. NICE advises **urgent referral** when the small joints of the hands or feet are involved, when several joints are inflamed, or when symptoms have lasted over 3 months.

blocks.title: Davidson's step-up pathway
rows: **Prednisolone 30 mg daily**, cut by 5 mg every 2 weeks (off by about 12 weeks) **plus methotrexate 15 mg weekly** with folic acid 5 mg weekly, raised to a maximum of 25 mg weekly
**Triple therapy**: MTX + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine; other DMARDs or low-dose prednisolone 5–10 mg may be added
Add a **biologic**, usually a **TNF inhibitor** first; JAK inhibitors are an alternative
TNF inhibitor fails: switch to a non-TNF biologic (rituximab, abatacept, tocilizumab)
Consider **reducing the biologic dose** (possible in up to 50%)
Sustained flare: change DMARD or biologic

blocks.alt: Algorithm: new RA starts prednisolone taper plus methotrexate. If DAS28 stays above 2.6 add sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine. Then DAS28 below 2.6 continue, 2.6 to 5.1 change DMARD or add low-dose prednisolone, above 5.1 add a biologic.

blocks.title: Bridging and symptom control
items: DMARDs take weeks to work (benefit often at 4–8 weeks, maximal by 1–3 months), so cover the gap with a **short glucocorticoid** course, **IM depot methylprednisolone 80–120 mg**, or NSAIDs, then taper.
NSAIDs relieve pain and stiffness but **do not slow** joint damage; give a **PPI** if over 65 or at GI risk.
One or two persistently active joints: **intra-articular glucocorticoid**; repeated injections into the same joint are avoided.
Methotrexate can be given **subcutaneously** if oral dosing causes nausea or is poorly absorbed.

blocks.title: Before and during biologic therapy
items: Screen for **TB** (history, chest X-ray, IGRA) and for **hepatitis B and C**; treat latent TB first.
Vaccinate against pneumococcus, influenza (annually) and zoster.
Usually co-prescribe **methotrexate**: it increases efficacy and reduces anti-drug antibodies.
**Never combine two biologics.**

blocks.title: RA and pregnancy
rows: Many women go into remission in pregnancy; RA may first appear post-partum
**MTX at least 3 months** (in men and women); **leflunomide at least 2 years**
**Paracetamol** first choice; NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors only from implantation to 20 weeks
Limited data; neonatal immunosuppression is the main concern; certolizumab barely crosses the placenta

blocks.title: Non-drug measures and surgery
items: MDT: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, specialist nurses, podiatry, psychology.
**Stop smoking** to reduce cardiovascular risk.

Surgery: synovectomy for resistant joints (eases pain and swelling but does not stop radiographic progression), joint replacement, excision of MTP heads, wrist or ankle fusion, neurosurgical fixation for atlanto-axial subluxation.

blocks.text: Books differ on when to start anti-TNF: **Davidson** adds a biologic when DAS28 stays **above 5.1 despite triple therapy**; Kumar says after **two conventional DMARDs** have failed; the NICE ladder in Zero to Finals uses MTX + biologic as the 3rd line. Davidson also starts MTX at 15 mg weekly where Kumar starts at 7.5–10 mg. Follow Davidson.
Sulfasalazine suits milder disease and women planning a family; methotrexate is the anchor drug for active disease unless CKD, liver disease, heavy alcohol use or lung disease make it unsuitable.

blocks.title: Conventional and targeted synthetic DMARDs
rows: Inhibits **dihydrofolate reductase**, so less tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis in leucocytes
Nausea/malaise 1–2 days after dose, mouth ulcers, hepatotoxicity, cytopenias (**macrocytic anaemia**), rare pneumonitis or pulmonary fibrosis; teratogenic
Weekly dose; folic acid 5 mg weekly on another day cuts side-effects; avoid excess alcohol; interacts with sulphonamides; FBC + LFTs
GI upset, rash, leucopenia, abnormal LFTs, mouth ulcers, **reversible male infertility**, orange urine and contact lenses
Check G6PD first; FBC + LFTs; safe in pregnancy
Not fully understood; interferes with Toll-like receptors and antigen presentation, raises lysosomal pH
**Retinal toxicity** with long use; haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Visual checks at baseline and periodically; safe in pregnancy
Inhibits **dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase**, blocking pyrimidine synthesis in activated lymphocytes
Liver dysfunction, **hypertension**, hirsutism, diarrhoea, alopecia; low marrow toxicity
Check BP; stop 2 years before pregnancy
Converted to **6-mercaptopurine**, which blocks DNA synthesis
TPMT variants affect toxicity; with **allopurinol** reduce dose by 75%
Block **Janus kinase** signalling inside the cell for several cytokines
Opportunistic infection (e.g. **herpes zoster**), hepatotoxicity, cytopenias, dyslipidaemia, VTE

blocks.title: Biologics
rows: Infection (the main risk of all biologics)
**Monoclonal antibodies** to TNF-α (infliximab chimeric, IV, given with MTX to limit anti-drug antibodies)
TB and hepatitis B reactivation, sepsis, worsening heart failure, demyelination, reversible lupus-like syndrome
Anti-**CD20**: complement-mediated B-cell depletion for months
Infusion reactions, hypogammaglobulinaemia, infections, rarely **PML** (JC virus)
**CTLA4-Ig** fusion protein blocking CD28 co-stimulation of T cells
Leucopenia, abnormal LFTs, hypercholesterolaemia, diverticulitis and GI perforation

blocks.text: **Anti-TNF contraindications:** active infection including untreated TB, indwelling catheters, **severe heart failure** and **multiple sclerosis**.

**MTX pneumonitis** can occur at any time: new cough or breathlessness means stop the drug and give high-dose glucocorticoids. A **macrocytic anaemia** in a patient on MTX reflects its antifolate action.

blocks.title: Glucocorticoids and NSAIDs
items: Long-term steroids: weight gain, thin skin, diabetes, hypertension, cataract, **osteoporosis**; give vitamin D and a bisphosphonate if use is expected beyond 3 months.
An NSAID plus a steroid greatly increases GI bleeding risk.
Biologics are not carcinogenic, but an existing cancer may progress faster under immunosuppression.

blocks.text: **Certolizumab pegol** is a PEGylated Fab fragment with **no Fc portion**, so very little crosses the placenta or enters breast milk.

blocks.note: Use it to link drugs to targets: T/B cell interaction, TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 from macrophages, and RANKL/M-CSF driving osteoclast erosion.

cards.front: Which hand joints does RA typically spare?
cards.back: The **DIP** joints (MCPs, PIPs and wrists are involved).

cards.front: Swan-neck deformity: position of MCP, PIP and DIP?
cards.back: The **PIP over-extends**; the DIP and MCP are both bent.

cards.front: A red, hot joint in a patient with RA should make you think of?
cards.back: **Septic arthritis**: erythema is unusual in RA; aspirate before calling it a flare.

cards.front: How long does acute viral polyarthritis usually last, and what is its ACPA status?
cards.back: Usually settles within about **6 weeks**; **ACPA negative**.

cards.front: 2010 ACR/EULAR: what total score classifies definite RA?
ACR/EULAR points for more than 10 joints with at least one small joint?
cards.back: **5 points** (the maximum for the joint domain).
**RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia**, usually long-standing seropositive, inactive deforming disease.
Rheumatoid lung nodules (may cavitate) in a patient with **pneumoconiosis**.

cards.front: Pleural fluid glucose in rheumatoid effusion?
ACPA sensitivity and specificity for RA (Davidson)?
New occipital headache with electric-shock arm sensations in RA?
cards.back: Suspect **atlanto-axial subluxation**: flexion/extension lateral X-rays + MRI, urgent neurosurgery if cord compressed.

cards.front: RA patient develops nephrotic syndrome. Likely complication?
Davidson's starting regimen for newly diagnosed RA?
cards.back: Prednisolone 30 mg tapered by 5 mg every 2 weeks + **methotrexate 15 mg weekly** with folic acid 5 mg weekly (up to 25 mg).

cards.front: Washout before conception for MTX and leflunomide?
cards.back: MTX at least **3 months**; leflunomide at least **2 years**.
Inhibits **dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase**, blocking pyrimidine synthesis in lymphocytes.
**CTLA4-Ig** fusion protein that blocks CD28 co-stimulation, so T cells are not activated.
Active infection or untreated TB, indwelling catheters, severe heart failure, multiple sclerosis.

questions.theme: Hand, wrist and limb findings in rheumatoid arthritis
options: Ulnar deviation at the MCP joints
Rupture of the 4th and 5th extensor tendons

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with 20 years of RA suddenly cannot straighten her ring and little fingers at the knuckles after lifting a pan. The ulnar head is prominent on the back of her wrist. Passive extension of the fingers is full.
items.explanation: The ulnar head, subluxed dorsally at the distal radio-ulnar joint, wears through the **4th and 5th extensor tendons**; sudden loss of active extension with full passive range means tendon rupture, not joint deformity.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with RA has a finger that is bent at the PIP joint while the DIP joint is pushed into extension.
items.explanation: **PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension** is the boutonnière ("button-hole") deformity. Swan neck is the reverse at PIP and DIP.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with RA and a chronically swollen right knee feels a sudden pain behind the knee while squatting. Within hours his calf is tense, swollen and tender. A compression ultrasound of the leg veins is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: calf swelling suggests DVT, but normal venous imaging plus knee synovitis and a popping pain behind the knee point to a **ruptured Baker's cyst**, which mimics DVT.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old nursery teacher has had painful swelling of both wrists and several MCP and PIP joints for 12 days, with morning stiffness. Several children at work were recently unwell with a viral illness. ACPA is negative; serology shows IgM antibodies to parvovirus (erythrovirus) B19.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A **short history** (under 6 weeks) of symmetrical small-joint arthritis with recent parvovirus infection and **negative ACPA** is a viral polyarthritis. These usually settle within about 6 weeks; persistence would prompt re-evaluation for RA.
whyNot: Possible pattern, but under 6 weeks of symptoms, negative ACPA and positive parvovirus IgM favour a viral cause, which is a recognised mimic of early RA.
Psoriatic arthritis tends to involve DIPs asymmetrically with dactylitis or nail changes.
Nodal OA gives bony DIP, PIP and thumb-base swelling, usually in older people, and would not explain a positive parvovirus IgM.
PMR affects older patients with proximal girdle stiffness, not small hand joints.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has painful swelling of the DIP and PIP joints of his left hand and one diffusely swollen, sausage-like toe. His nails show small pits. RF and ACPA are negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **DIP involvement, asymmetry, dactylitis and nail pitting** are the hallmarks of psoriatic arthritis, even before skin psoriasis appears.
whyNot: RA is symmetrical and spares the DIPs; dactylitis and nail pitting are not features.
Nodal OA causes bony DIP/PIP nodes without dactylitis or nail pitting.
Viral polyarthritis is symmetrical, short-lived and does not cause nail pitting.
Palindromic attacks resolve completely within 1–2 days.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had swelling of 12 joints, including several MCPs and MTPs, for 8 weeks. RF and ACPA are both negative. CRP is raised.
questions.leadIn: What is her total 2010 ACR/EULAR score?
questions.explanation: More than 10 joints with at least one small joint = **5**; negative serology = **0**; over 6 weeks = **1**; raised CRP = **1**. Total **7**, so she meets the criteria for definite RA despite being seronegative.
whyNot: Too low: more than 10 joints including a small one scores 5 on its own, so the total cannot fall below 5.
This counts only the joint domain.
This misses one of the 1-point domains (duration or CRP).
Serology is negative and scores 0, so 8 is not reachable.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has had swelling of three MCP joints for 4 weeks. ACPA is strongly positive. CRP and ESR are normal. His ACR/EULAR score is 5.
questions.leadIn: Which single further finding would bring him to the classification threshold?
options: A marginal erosion on hand X-ray
questions.explanation: He scores 2 (1–3 small joints) + 3 (high-positive ACPA) = 5. Passing **6 weeks** adds 1 point, giving **6** = definite RA.
whyNot: Adding a large joint keeps him in the 1–3 small joints category (2 points).
Serology already scores the maximum 3; a low-positive RF adds nothing.
Stiffness duration is not a scored domain.
Erosions are not part of the 2010 scoring; the criteria were designed not to need them.

questions.leadIn: Choose the best match from the list for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has 25 years of high-titre RF-positive RA. Her hands are deformed but her joints are not currently swollen. She has had three chest infections this year. The spleen tip is palpable and the neutrophil count is 0.8 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: Long-standing seropositive, **deforming but inactive** disease with **splenomegaly and neutropenia** (and recurrent infection) is Felty's syndrome.

items.stem: A 59-year-old retired coal miner with RA has a chest X-ray showing several well-defined 1–2 cm peripheral nodules, two of which have cavitated.
items.explanation: Rheumatoid lung nodules in a patient with **pneumoconiosis** = Caplan's syndrome.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman with RA has a deep, boring pain in her right eye that keeps her awake. The eye is red and tender to touch, and her vision is slightly blurred.
items.explanation: A **painful** red eye with tenderness and visual change is scleritis, a sight-threatening complication, unlike the painless gritty dryness of sicca.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with seropositive nodular RA has small dark infarcts at his nail folds. Over three weeks he develops a right foot drop, then weakness of left wrist extension.
items.explanation: Two steps: nail-fold infarcts signal **rheumatoid vasculitis**; separate named nerves failing one after another is **mononeuritis multiplex** from nerve-trunk infarction, a poor prognostic sign.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has 5 weeks of hand pain. She also reports dry eyes and a dry mouth. Examination of her hands is equivocal. Rheumatoid factor is strongly positive.
questions.leadIn: Which blood test best tells whether the positive RF reflects rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation: RF is positive in about 90% of **Sjögren's** and in many other conditions. **ACPA** has similar sensitivity (~70%) but **specificity over 95%**, so it is the test that supports RA.
whyNot: ANA is non-specific and is also positive in Sjögren's and RA.
RF titre neither separates RA from Sjögren's nor changes much over time.
ESR reflects inflammation of any cause.
FBC may show anaemia of chronic disease but is not specific.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with RF-positive RA diagnosed 2 years ago presents with increasing joint pain and swelling.
questions.leadIn: Which blood test best tracks his current level of inflammatory activity?
questions.explanation: **ESR and CRP** rise and fall with disease activity and feed into DAS28. RF titres change little with activity.
whyNot: RF titre rarely changes with activity; a high titre only predicts more severe disease.
ACPA is a diagnostic and prognostic marker, not a monitoring test.
ANA is found at low titre in some RA patients and does not track activity.
Urate is for gout and has no role in monitoring RA.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with 18 years of erosive RA has a new headache at the back of her head. When she bends her neck forward she feels electric-shock sensations down both arms. Hand power is hard to test because of deformity.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate investigation?
options: Lateral cervical spine X-rays in flexion and extension, then MRI
Nerve conduction studies of both median nerves
questions.explanation: New **occipital headache with electric-shock arm symptoms** in long-standing RA suggests **atlanto-axial subluxation**. Dynamic lateral films and MRI show instability and cord compression; compression needs urgent neurosurgery.
whyNot: Carpal tunnel gives hand paraesthesia, not neck-triggered shocks with headache.
The problem is at C1–C2, not intracranial.
RF titre does not assess the cervical spine.
There is no suggestion of meningitis, and LP does not image the cord.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with 30 years of RA, taking methotrexate and paracetamol, develops leg oedema. Urine protein is 6 g/day and serum albumin is 21 g/L. His joint disease has been active for most of that time.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Long-standing active RA is the commonest cause of **secondary AA amyloidosis**, which usually presents with **nephrotic syndrome**.
whyNot: Analgesic nephropathy is a recognised renal problem in RA, but nephrotic syndrome in long-standing active disease is the classic presentation of AA amyloid.
Felty's causes splenomegaly and neutropenia, not nephrotic syndrome.
Pleural disease does not explain proteinuria.
Cervical subluxation causes neurological, not renal, problems.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with ACPA-positive RA affecting both hands and feet. She has normal renal and liver function, drinks no alcohol and has a normal chest X-ray.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the best initial treatment?
options: Prednisolone 30 mg daily, tapered over about 12 weeks, plus weekly methotrexate with folic acid
Regular NSAID with a proton pump inhibitor alone until erosions appear
questions.explanation: Davidson starts **prednisolone 30 mg** (cut by 5 mg every 2 weeks) together with **methotrexate 15 mg weekly** and folic acid 5 mg weekly, increasing MTX to 25 mg if needed. Early DMARD therapy improves outcome.
whyNot: NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not prevent damage; waiting for erosions loses the window.
Biologics come after conventional DMARDs fail.
HCQ alone is reserved for mild disease; this patient needs MTX.
Rituximab is typically third-line after TNF inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has taken methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine at full doses for 6 months. His DAS28 is 5.7. Chest X-ray and IGRA are negative, and hepatitis B and C serology is negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add a TNF inhibitor to methotrexate
Continue triple therapy and review in 3 months
Add a second biologic alongside a TNF inhibitor
Stop all DMARDs and give prednisolone alone
Start rituximab as the first biologic
questions.explanation: DAS28 **above 5.1 despite triple therapy** is the Davidson trigger for a **biologic**, usually a TNF inhibitor co-prescribed with MTX after negative TB and hepatitis screening.
whyNot: Continuing unchanged accepts high disease activity and further damage.
Two biologics must never be combined.
Steroid monotherapy does not control RA and causes long-term harm.
Rituximab is typically used after TNF inhibitors have failed.

questions.leadIn: Choose the best match from the list for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.
questions.theme: Adverse effects of drugs used in rheumatoid arthritis

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with RA notices that her soft contact lenses and her urine have turned orange since she started a new tablet.
items.explanation: **Orange staining** of urine and contact lenses is characteristic of sulfasalazine.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with RA develops a dry cough and increasing breathlessness. He takes a tablet once a week with folic acid on another day. CT shows new bilateral ground-glass change.
items.explanation: Weekly dosing with folic acid identifies **methotrexate**; new cough and breathlessness suggest MTX **pneumonitis**: stop the drug and give high-dose steroids.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with RA has a new BP of 162/98 mmHg and increased facial hair. She now wants to conceive and is told this drug must be stopped 2 years before she tries.
items.explanation: **Hypertension and hirsutism**, plus a **2-year** pre-conception stop, point to leflunomide.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman with RA has an abnormal finding at her periodic eye check after 8 years of a once-daily tablet that was chosen partly because it is safe in pregnancy and needs no routine blood monitoring.
items.explanation: No routine blood tests, safe in pregnancy and **visual function** monitoring = hydroxychloroquine, which can accumulate in the retina.

questions.leadIn: Choose the best match from the list for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.
questions.theme: Mechanisms of action of drugs used in RA
options: Antibody to CD20 causing B-cell depletion

items.stem: A patient with RA injects a weekly fusion protein that mops up circulating TNF-α before it reaches cell-surface receptors.
items.explanation: Etanercept is a **decoy receptor** for TNF-α, unlike the monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies.

items.stem: After several treatment courses for RA a 66-year-old man has low immunoglobulin levels. He then develops progressive confusion and hemiparesis; JC virus is found in his CSF.
items.explanation: Hypogammaglobulinaemia and **PML (JC virus)** are recognised effects of rituximab, an **anti-CD20** B-cell-depleting antibody.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman with RA develops shingles 3 months after starting an oral tablet taken twice daily that blocks cytokine signalling inside the cell.
items.explanation: Oral twice-daily tofacitinib is a **JAK inhibitor**; herpes zoster is a typical infection risk.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman with RA has a raised cholesterol and mild neutropenia after starting a new biologic, and is then admitted with perforated diverticulitis.
items.explanation: Two steps: hypercholesterolaemia, leucopenia and **diverticulitis/GI perforation** identify tocilizumab, whose target is the **IL-6 receptor**.

questions.leadIn: Choose the best match from the list for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.
questions.theme: Choosing the next investigation in rheumatoid arthritis
options: Plain X-rays of hands and feet
Joint aspiration with Gram stain and culture
Chest X-ray and interferon-gamma release assay
Full blood count and liver function tests

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman with RA on methotrexate has one hot, red, very painful knee. Her other joints are quiet. She has no fever.
items.explanation: Two steps: a single joint flaring out of proportion, with redness, is septic until proven otherwise; immunosuppression can blunt fever. **Aspirate** before treating as a flare.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man with RA is about to start adalimumab after failing triple therapy.
items.explanation: Before anti-TNF therapy, screen for **TB** with a chest X-ray and IGRA (and hepatitis B and C).

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has 2 months of early-morning hand stiffness and pain. On examination the MCPs are tender, but it is unclear whether there is swelling.
items.explanation: **Ultrasound** (or MRI) helps when synovitis is clinically uncertain.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with mild RA is to start a DMARD that does not need routine blood monitoring but can accumulate in the retina.
items.explanation: Hydroxychloroquine needs a **baseline visual check** repeated periodically.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with RA has been taking a weekly DMARD for 2 years. She has become tired. Hb is 94 g/L with an MCV of 109 fL. She admits she often forgets her folic acid tablets.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most likely responsible for her anaemia?
questions.explanation: Step 1: classify the anaemia: MCV over 100 fL is **macrocytic**. Step 2: RA itself gives a normocytic anaemia, and NSAID blood loss gives a microcytic one, so a macrocytic picture points to a drug. Step 3: **methotrexate** inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so it causes folate-deficient (megaloblastic) marrow changes; missed folic acid makes this more likely. Step 4: check FBC and LFTs and review dosing.
whyNot: HCQ is mainly linked to retinal toxicity; it causes haemolysis only in G6PD deficiency.
Sulfasalazine is linked mainly to GI upset and leucopenia; macrocytic anaemia is the classic methotrexate clue.
Steroids do not cause macrocytic anaemia.
Etanercept's main risk is infection.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with well-controlled RA on methotrexate and leflunomide wants to try for a baby within the next year.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate DMARD plan?
options: Stop both drugs and switch to sulfasalazine with hydroxychloroquine
Continue both drugs until a pregnancy test is positive
Stop methotrexate and continue leflunomide alone
questions.explanation: Step 1: list the teratogens: MTX (stop at least **3 months** before conception) and leflunomide (long half-life; stop **2 years** ahead). Step 2: list drugs compatible with pregnancy: **sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, azathioprine**. Step 3: switch to SSZ + HCQ to keep disease controlled; paracetamol is the analgesic of choice.
whyNot: Stopping only at a positive test exposes the embryo to two teratogens.
Leflunomide must be stopped long before conception.
Mycophenolate must be avoided in pregnancy.
Cyclophosphamide must be avoided in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with RA takes naproxen daily and methotrexate. She feels breathless on stairs. Hb is 88 g/L, MCV 71 fL, platelets 410 × 10⁹/L, ferritin low.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
options: Iron deficiency from NSAID-related GI blood loss
questions.explanation: Step 1: MCV 71 fL is **microcytic**. Step 2: anaemia of active RA is usually normocytic with thrombocytosis, and MTX causes macrocytosis. Step 3: low ferritin confirms **iron deficiency**, and a daily NSAID is the likely source of GI loss. Next: stop or protect (PPI) and investigate the GI tract.
whyNot: Anaemia of active RA is normochromic and normocytic, often with thrombocytosis; it does not explain an MCV of 71 fL with low ferritin.
MTX gives a macrocytic, not microcytic, picture.
Felty's causes cytopenias with splenomegaly and neutropenia, not iron deficiency.
Haemolysis would not give a low ferritin and microcytosis.

questions.leadIn: Choose the best match from the list for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has 4 months of symmetrical swelling of the MCP and PIP joints and both wrists, with 2 hours of morning stiffness. The DIPs are normal and ACPA is positive.
items.explanation: Symmetrical MCP/PIP/wrist synovitis sparing the DIPs, prolonged stiffness and **ACPA positivity** over months is RA.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man has had several attacks over a year: one day his left knee is red and swollen, two weeks later his right wrist; each attack settles completely within 2 days. Between attacks he is well. RF is positive.
items.explanation: Brief attacks lasting 24–48 h in different joints, resolving fully, are **palindromic rheumatism**; positive RF (or ACPA) predicts progression to RA.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has hard, bony swellings at the DIP and PIP joints and pain at the base of the thumb. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes and CRP is normal.
items.explanation: Bony nodes at DIPs and PIPs, thumb-base pain, brief stiffness and normal CRP = **nodal OA**.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has a swollen right knee and left ankle and pain at the heel where the Achilles tendon inserts. His hands are normal and RF and ACPA are negative.
items.explanation: Asymmetrical **large lower-limb joints** with enthesitis and negative serology suggest a spondyloarthritis, not RA.

questions.leadIn: Choose the best match from the list for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.
questions.theme: Next treatment step in rheumatoid arthritis
options: Prednisolone taper plus methotrexate with folic acid
Add sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine to methotrexate

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman is diagnosed today with seropositive RA of the hands and feet. Bloods and chest X-ray are normal.
items.explanation: Davidson starts **prednisolone 30 mg tapered over ~12 weeks with methotrexate 15 mg weekly** plus folic acid at diagnosis.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has taken methotrexate 25 mg weekly for 3 months. His DAS28 is 4.3.
items.explanation: DAS28 still above 2.6 on MTX: move to **triple therapy** (add SSZ + HCQ).

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has used triple therapy for 6 months; DAS28 is 5.9. TB and hepatitis screens are negative.
items.explanation: DAS28 above 5.1 despite triple therapy: add a biologic, usually a **TNF inhibitor**.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man feels sick and washed-out for two days after each weekly methotrexate tablet. His arthritis is well controlled.
items.explanation: Nausea and malaise 1–2 days after oral MTX may be avoided with **subcutaneous** dosing.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman in remission on combination therapy has had a persistent effusion of one knee for 4 weeks. Aspirate is sterile.
items.explanation: One problem joint with good overall control: **intra-articular glucocorticoid** (sepsis has been excluded).

questions.leadIn: Choose the best match from the list for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.
questions.theme: Complications of rheumatoid arthritis and its treatment
options: Iron deficiency from NSAID GI blood loss

items.stem: A 55-year-old man from a high-TB region started infliximab 4 months ago. He has 6 weeks of fever, night sweats and weight loss, and a cavity in the right upper lobe.
items.explanation: Anti-TNF therapy can **reactivate latent TB**, hence the pre-treatment screening.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with 25 years of RA has firm, painless, enlarging lymph nodes in her neck and axilla for 4 months, although her joints are currently quiet.
items.explanation: Lymphadenopathy can occur with active RA, but **persistent** enlarging nodes with quiet joints suggest **lymphoma**, which is more common in long-standing RA.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman taking etanercept develops new arthralgia, a facial rash and a positive ANA; her symptoms resolve after the drug is stopped.
items.explanation: TNF blockers can cause a **reversible lupus-like syndrome**.

items.stem: A 73-year-old woman with RA has taken prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 8 years without other bone treatment. She develops sudden severe mid-back pain after lifting a shopping bag.
items.explanation: Two steps: RA and long-term steroids both cause **osteoporosis**; sudden back pain after a trivial strain is a **vertebral fragility fracture**. Steroid users expected to need treatment beyond 3 months should get bone protection.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with RA is stable on azathioprine 150 mg daily. She develops recurrent gout and her GP plans to start allopurinol.
questions.leadIn: What change to her azathioprine is needed?
options: Give the same dose on alternate days only
questions.explanation: Allopurinol blocks the breakdown of azathioprine (6-mercaptopurine), so marrow toxicity rises unless the azathioprine dose is **cut by about 75%**.
whyNot: Leaving the dose unchanged risks severe marrow suppression.
Increasing the dose worsens toxicity.
Alternate-day dosing halves exposure, which is not enough reduction.
Timing does not change the interaction.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has dry eyes and dry mouth for 2 years. She has no joint swelling. RF is strongly positive and ACPA is negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for her positive rheumatoid factor?
questions.explanation: RF is positive in about **90% of Sjögren's syndrome**. With sicca symptoms, no synovitis and **negative ACPA**, Sjögren's explains it best.
whyNot: No synovitis and a negative ACPA make RA unlikely.
Only about 30% of SLE patients are RF positive, and nothing here suggests lupus.
TB causes RF positivity in about 15%, but she has no features of infection.
Age-related RF positivity is mainly in people over 65 and would not explain sicca symptoms.

questions.leadIn: Choose the best match from the list for each patient. An option may fit several patients, or none.
questions.theme: Blood results in patients with rheumatoid arthritis
options: Anaemia of chronic disease with reactive thrombocytosis

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with very active RA (DAS28 6.1) has Hb 101 g/L, MCV 86 fL, platelets 560 × 10⁹/L and CRP 74 mg/L.
items.explanation: A **normocytic** anaemia with **thrombocytosis** tracking high CRP is the anaemia of active inflammation.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man of Mediterranean origin starts a DMARD that is not usually monitored with blood tests. Two weeks later he is jaundiced with a falling Hb and a raised reticulocyte count.
items.explanation: Two steps: a DMARD without routine blood monitoring is **hydroxychloroquine**; jaundice with reticulocytosis is **haemolysis**, which HCQ can trigger in G6PD deficiency.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with RA has received four courses of a B-cell-depleting infusion. He now has recurrent chest infections and a low serum IgG.
items.explanation: Rituximab depletes CD20 B cells and can cause **hypogammaglobulinaemia** and infection.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman with 22 years of erosive RA is listed for elective hip replacement under general anaesthesia. She has no neck pain or neurological symptoms.
questions.leadIn: Which pre-operative investigation is most important because of her RA?
options: Flexion and extension lateral cervical spine imaging
questions.explanation: Cervical instability is common in long-standing RA and may be silent; neck movement during **intubation** can injure the cord. Flexion/extension imaging (with MRI if abnormal) is recommended before surgery.
whyNot: Lung function testing is not the RA-specific safety priority here.
Bone density is useful for osteoporosis but does not change anaesthetic safety.
She has no neuropathic symptoms.
Antibody titres do not affect surgical risk.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with RA has high disease activity despite triple therapy. His rheumatologist wants to start a biologic. TB screening is negative.
questions.leadIn: Which feature of his history is a contraindication to anti-TNF therapy?
questions.explanation: Anti-TNF drugs can worsen **severe heart failure** and **multiple sclerosis**, and must not be given with active infection, untreated TB or indwelling catheters.
whyNot: Hypertension is not a contraindication (it matters more for leflunomide).
Diabetes alone does not preclude anti-TNF therapy.
Past surgery is irrelevant.
Coexisting OA is not a contraindication.

ospe.identify: Rheumatoid hand: **ulnar deviation** at the MCPs, small-muscle wasting, swelling of wrists, extensor sheaths, MCPs and PIPs; **swan-neck** fingers (PIP hyperextension).
Established RA hand deformities (ulnar deviation, boutonnière, swan neck) and, in early disease, dorsal wrist tenosynovitis with **spindle-shaped** fingers.
**Rheumatoid nodules** at the elbow with olecranon bursitis: firm subcutaneous nodules over an extensor pressure point, a marker of seropositive disease.
Hand X-ray in early RA: **marginal erosions** at the thumb, middle MCP joints and ulnar styloid.
OA vs RA hand films: OA shows **osteophytes**, subchondral sclerosis and narrowing; RA shows **periarticular erosions and osteopenia**.
**Atlanto-axial subluxation**: on flexion the gap between the odontoid peg and the anterior arch of the atlas widens; on extension it closes.
